title: Warn the door
script: MARA: That cabinet is already smoking. Stop the pump before it catches.
JOHN: Someone’s at the pressure door. Give me one call to clear them first.
MARA: One call. If it sparks again, I’m hitting the stop.
notes: Both risks are immediate. A warning can protect someone before shutdown. Cassidy A identifies the contact at Loading; John B explores the alternative.

title: Stop the pump
script: IVO: If you hit that stop, the gallery door shuts. Someone might be crossing it.
JOHN: That cabinet is arcing. Get back—I’m stopping it now.
IVO: Then tell me who’s on the other side!
notes: Stopping prevents an electrical fire but can close the door with someone near it. The door indicators and Cassidy A give context; good preparation can preserve both outcomes.

title: Compare the readings
script: NELL: That level sensor has drifted before. We could shut off good water over a bad reading.
PRUE: I’m comparing it to the flow meter. If they agree, the tank is still filling.
NELL: And if they don’t, we’ve lost time.
notes: The level and independent flow meter agree: water is entering. It does not identify the route. Combine with Cassidy B or Act 2 Prue A; direct inspection also works.

title: Trust the display
script: NELL: The level is still going up. We have to find where the water is coming from.
PRUE: Control says its intake valve is closed. This sensor has drifted before—I’m checking it first.
NELL: If it’s right this time, the tank keeps filling while you check.
notes: The display accurately reports the Control valve, not the separate transfer path. Checking a suspect sensor is reasonable, but assuming all intake is stopped is incomplete. Prue A and Cassidy B add independent facts.

title: Call Loading
script: MARA: The cabinet is sparking! We can’t wait for everyone to check in.
CASSIDY: Tavi answered from Loading. If that stop closes the door, she may be on the far side.
MARA: And if the cabinet catches, we may lose the whole passage.
notes: Cassidy identifies Tavi’s location, not a guaranteed position in the current timeline. John A or B identifies the door/pump relationship. Calling Tavi can quickly resolve the uncertainty.

title: Follow the sound
script: NELL: The intake display says closed. That sound could be any pipe in Loading.
CASSIDY: Tavi says she can hear water running beside her hatch. I’m going to find out which pipe.
NELL: If you go, who’s checking whether the tank level is real?
notes: Tavi’s report locates a sound but does not establish its function. Prue A establishes rising tank and flow; Act 2 Prue A traces the physical connection.

title: Equalize the hatch
script: TAVI: The water’s rising in here. Just open it!
JOHN: The pressure marker’s red. I’m equalizing it before I move the hatch.
TAVI: How long is that going to take?
notes: Tavi needs help urgently; opening against unequal pressure can flood the passage. Cassidy A identifies which side water is on; direct readings and other rescue approaches remain valid.

title: Open the hatch
script: IVO: That marker is red. Opening it could send water straight through the passage.
JOHN: Tavi is trapped and the water’s climbing. Stand clear—I’m opening it.
IVO: John, wait. We can try the equalization valve—
notes: A fast rescue is a credible reason to act; uncontrolled opening risks a surge. Stop the clip before a predetermined outcome. Cassidy A provides the trapped worker’s position.

title: Trace the line
script: IVO: That line supplies us. If you shut it, we lose water we may need.
PRUE: I’m tracing it first. It runs around the valve Control is showing us.
IVO: If it goes where you think, close it—but check before you turn it.
notes: Prue establishes a bypass route, not the valve’s location. Combine Cassidy B (Tavi’s Loading report) and the local flow indicator before deciding what to close.

title: Keep the supply open
script: MARA: Water is still moving near Loading. We need to stop it before the tank fills.
PRUE: We don’t know which line that is yet, and the crew still needs water. I’m leaving it until we confirm it.
MARA: Then find out fast. The level isn’t waiting.
notes: Preserving a water supply is reasonable; leaving the bypass open permits continued inflow. Prue A and Cassidy B establish route and location. An independent physical trace is valid.

title: Find Tavi’s position
script: TAVI: I’m behind the loading hatch! Stop talking and open it!
CASSIDY: Is the water against your side of the hatch, or in the passage?
TAVI: My side. It’s at my knees—please hurry.
notes: Tavi knows her own position and water level, not the complete pressure diagnosis. John A/B and the marker connect that observation to the hatch decision.

title: Evacuate before the report
script: TAVI: There’s an open valve by the pipe—I can show you which one.
CASSIDY: You’re shaking and the passage is filling. I’m getting you to the shuttle first.
TAVI: Then listen while we move! That line is still running.
notes: Evacuating is sensible and listening while moving may preserve both objectives. Tavi provides the Loading valve’s location, while Prue A identifies the bypass route. Pipe labels and gauges are alternate evidence.

title: Clear the analyzer
script: IVO: Leave the analyzer. Moving it will pull that damaged pipe bracket.
JOHN: It’s blocking the route, and we need the unit out. I’ll support the bracket while we move it.
IVO: If there’s pressure in that pipe, a brace may not be enough.
notes: John locates the damaged obstruction but does not identify the pipe. Cassidy A identifies it as the relief line; gauge and valve checks establish whether it is safe to move.

title: Use the lift
script: IVO: Don’t restore that circuit until we know what else is on it.
JOHN: The manual lift is slow, and the analyzer is blocking our way out. We need power.
IVO: If the pump starts again, that tank takes the load.
notes: The lift is useful. Prue A/B and the local controller identify a separate armed restart. Check or isolate it first, use the manual crank, or choose another viable approach.

title: Inspect the controller
script: MARA: If you cut that circuit, we could lose the lift while the tank’s still under pressure.
PRUE: Control’s timer is canceled, but there’s a second controller here. I’m checking what the armed light means.
MARA: Check fast. We still need a way out.
notes: Prue identifies a second controller and armed indicator, not a complete conclusion. John B links power restoration to the lift circuit; the diagram, a direct test or Ivo can establish the restart function.

title: Restore the circuit
script: IVO: There’s still an armed light on the pump controller. Don’t reset the circuit yet.
PRUE: I canceled the schedule at Control. We need the lift power to move the analyzer.
IVO: What if that light means it can still restart locally?
notes: The Control timer is canceled but the separate local restart remains armed. Both want to move the equipment safely. Prue A and John B help connect the controller and shared power.

title: Identify the line
script: NELL: If we leave the relief valve closed, the tank stays under pressure.
CASSIDY: That split pipe beside the analyzer is the relief line. Check its pressure and isolation before we move it.
NELL: And if it’s still connected, how are we relieving the tank?
notes: Cassidy identifies the damaged pipe but does not prove isolation. Combine John A (obstruction) with local gauge and valve position; zero on one gauge alone is not proof of isolation.

title: Use the relief valve
script: NELL: That relief pipe is split. Opening the valve could flood our only clear route.
CASSIDY: The tank is under pressure. I want to open it a little while we watch the line.
NELL: How will we know it can take even that much?
notes: Controlled venting might be feasible with adequate inspection, repair or support; its success is not automatic. John A identifies the obstruction; Cassidy A identifies the relief line. Another outlet or stable hold may also work.
